title: Book 8 — Urania, Chapter 100
paragraphs: As for the Persians, this went on for the whole intervening period until the coming of Xerxes himself made them cease. Mardonius, seeing that Xerxes was greatly troubled by the sea-fight and suspecting that he meant to flee from Athens, considered, for himself, that he would have to pay the penalty for having persuaded the king to march against Greece, and that it was better for him to take the risk of either subduing Greece or ending his own life honorably, staking his safety on a great end — though his own opinion was rather that he would subdue Greece. Weighing all this, he addressed the king as follows: “Master, do not grieve, nor feel great distress over what has happened. For the outcome of all our fortunes does not depend on a contest of timbers, but of men and horses. None of those who now think they have achieved everything will try to disembark from their ships and stand against you, nor will anyone here on the mainland do so; those who did stand against us paid the penalty. If, then, you think it good to do so, let us at once attempt the Peloponnese; or if you think it better to hold back, we can do that. Do not despair: there is no escape for the Greeks but to become your slaves, after they have first given an account of what they did to you both now and before. That is the best course. But if you have indeed decided to withdraw yourself and take your army away, I have another counsel to offer in that case too. Do not, O king, let the Persians be an object of mockery to the Greeks; for nothing of yours has suffered through the Persians, nor can you name any place where we showed ourselves cowards. If Phoenicians, Egyptians, Cyprians, or Cilicians proved cowards, the calamity that followed has nothing to do with the Persians. Now, therefore, since the Persians are not guilty towards you, follow my counsel. If you have determined not to remain here, withdraw to your own home, taking with you the main body of the army, and it will then be for me to deliver over to you Greece subdued — choosing for this purpose three hundred thousand from the army.”
